content: Preterm premature rupture of membranes (PPROM) is a significant contributor to perinatal morbidity and mortality. Amnioinfusion is a medical procedure designed to replenish the amniotic fluid volume by introducing a solution into the uterine cavity. The purpose of this review was to evaluate the impact of amnioinfusion on both perinatal and maternal morbidity and mortality in cases of PPROM. The review involved a systematic search of the Cochrane Pregnancy and Childbirth Group's Trials Register as of December 2, 2013. Only randomized controlled trials comparing amnioinfusion with no amnioinfusion in women with PPROM were included. Three authors independently assessed the eligibility of trials, while two authors evaluated the quality of the studies and extracted data. The accuracy of the data was verified. Five trials of moderate quality were included in the review, but data from only four studies, involving a total of 241 participants, were analyzed. One trial did not provide usable data. The findings indicated that transcervical amnioinfusion improved fetal umbilical artery pH at delivery (mean difference 0.11; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.08 to 0.14; based on one trial with 61 participants). It also reduced the occurrence of persistent variable decelerations during labor (risk ratio [RR] 0.52; 95% CI 0.30 to 0.91; based on one trial with 86 participants). Transabdominal amnioinfusion was associated with several benefits. It significantly reduced the risk of neonatal death (RR 0.30; 95% CI 0.14 to 0.66; based on two trials with 94 participants), neonatal sepsis (RR 0.26; 95% CI 0.11 to 0.61; based on one trial with 60 participants), pulmonary hypoplasia (RR 0.22; 95% CI 0.06 to 0.88; based on one trial with 34 participants), and puerperal sepsis (RR 0.20; 95% CI 0.05 to 0.84; based on one trial with 60 participants). Additionally, women who underwent amnioinfusion were less likely to deliver within seven days of membrane rupture (RR 0.18; 95% CI 0.05 to 0.70; based on one trial with 34 participants). However, these findings should be interpreted with caution. The positive outcomes were primarily derived from a single trial with unclear allocation concealment, raising concerns about the reliability of the results. The authors concluded that while the results are promising, the limited data and methodological uncertainties necessitate further research before amnioinfusion for PPROM can be recommended as a standard clinical practice.
